newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhs to built new nuclear power stations.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhs to built new nuclear power stations.

text.p: Uranium-rich Kazakhstan, facing a shortage of electricity, plans to build two or three nuclear power stations by 2030 and a nuclear heating station, installing six nuclear reactors on its territory.
"These will be mostly stations of small and average capacity," Valerian Shemansky, deputy head of the state-owned Atomic Power Engineering and Industry Company, (KATEP) said.
KATEP, along with three uranium mines, a geological company and the Ulbinsky metals plant, will be part of the recently founded national atomic energy company Kazatomprom.
Shemansky told Reuters that the capacity of each of the six reactors to be installed in the former Soviet republic would be 640 megawatts and the building costs could reach $5.5 billion.

"Two thirds of the funds needed could be raised by inviting foreign investors," he said. "These stations are important for heavily industrialised Kazakhstan, whose regional shortages of electricity today may lead to a nationwide one by 2010."
He said that Russian pressurised water reactors VVER-640 were most likely to be installed at the future stations because foreign reactors were designed for higher power capacities.
Shemansky declined to say in what parts of Kazakhstan -- a Central Asian state five times the size of France and populated by just 16.7 million people -- all the stations would be built.
One, however, may be located near Lake Balkhash, some 400 km (250 miles) north of the capital, Almaty.

The decision to build the Balkhash nuclear power station could be taken by the Kazakh government no earlier than the middle of the next year after a special commission of experts had completed its feasibility study.

Shemansky said that a nuclear heating station could eventually be built in Almaty, allowing economies. The city of 1.5 million is now heated annually by 804,000 tonnes of coal, 371,000 tonnes of heating oil and 33,000 tonnes of liquid gas.

Kazakhstan, which holds a quarter of the world's reserves of uranium ores, produces 1,240 tonnes of uranium a year, exporting concentrate of uranium oxide-protoxide to the United States and fuel for atomic power stations to Russia, Ukraine and Bulgaria.
Kazakh officials say their country now ranks seventh among the world's exporters of uranium but give no precise data.
Kazakhstan has five reactors, four for scientific purposes. The fifth, in Aktau on the Caspian Sea, distils Caspian water and provides the town with electricity.
